rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The likeness concerns people already astray before revelation who remain astray after receiving guidance, gaining no benefit from it; they resemble the dog in the parable.
rows.anchor: مثل هؤلاء القوم الذين كانوا ضالين قبل أن تأتيهم بالهدى والرسالة ثم جئتهم بذلك فبقوا على ضلالتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to recount the stories recalls matters of the unseen known from earlier scriptures, inviting the listeners to reflect and believe.
rows.anchor: ما يعلمون أنه من الغيوب التي لا يعلمها إلا أهل الكتب الماضية ولست منهم لعلهم يتفكرون في ذلك فيؤمنون

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj supplies the implied wording “the likeness of the people” after sāʾa; what follows biʾsa or niʿma is interpreted from its own kind, as in “a bad man, Zayd.”
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: التقدير ساء مثلا مثل القوم، لأن الذي بعد «بئس» و «نعم» إنما يتفسر من نوعه

rows.speaker: الجحدري
rows.claim: Al-Jahdari reads “sāʾa mithlu al-qawmi,” with mithl in the nominative governed by sāʾa; on this reading sāʾa does not work like biʾsa unless its following noun is accusative.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجحدري «ساء مثل القوم، ورفع مثل على هذه القراءة ب ساء

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو الداني
rows.claim: Al-Dani reports al-Jahdari with mīm kasra and lām nominative, and al-Aʿmash with mīm and thāʾ fatḥa and lām nominative.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عمرو الداني: قرأ الجحدري «مثل» بكسر الميم ورفع اللام، وقرأ الأعمش «مثل» بفتح الميم والثاء ورفع اللام

rows.speaker: أبو حاتم
rows.claim: Abu Hatim instead says both al-Jahdari and al-Aʿmash read sāʾa mithlu with nominative inflection.
rows.anchor: فإنه قال: قرأ الجحدري والأعمش «ساء مثل» بالرفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage concludes that guidance and misguidance alike come from God’s creation, while reward and punishment attach to human beings’ acquired deeds.
rows.anchor: الهداية منه وبخلقه واختراعه وكذلك الإضلال، وفي الآية تعجب من حال المذكورين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account expresses wonder at the people’s condition and says that whoever is led astray is fixed upon loss.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية تعجب من حال المذكورين، ومن أضل فقد حتم عليه بالخسران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God reports that He created and brought many jinn and humans into being for Hell, a warning to disbelievers; dharaʾa means creating with dispersion and spreading.
rows.anchor: خبر من الله تعالى أنه خلق لسكنى جهنم والاحتراق فيها كثيرا، وفي ضمنه وعيد للكفار، و «ذرأ» معناه خلق وأوجد مع بث ونشر

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One group construes the lām in “for Hell” as a lām of consequence.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة اللام في قوله: لجهنم هي لام العاقبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya rejects the consequence reading: that construction applies when the actor did not intend the eventual result, whereas here the outcome of their dwelling in Hell was intended.
rows.anchor: وهذا ليس بصحيح ولام العاقبة إنما يتصور إذا كان فعل الفاعل لم يقصد به ما يصير الأمر إليه

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The author cites an anonymous poet’s line as an example of the lām construction, with a mother giving birth “for death.”
rows.anchor: فكل والدة للموت تلد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām here expresses an intended end: the act was meant to result in their dwelling in Hell, rather than merely producing an unintended consequence.
rows.anchor: وأما هنا فالفعل قصد به ما يصير الأمر إليه من سكناهم جهنم

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Al-Tabari reports Saʿid ibn Jubayr saying that children born of fornication are among those God created for Hell.
rows.anchor: عن سعيد بن جبير أنه قال أولاد الزنا مما ذرأ الله لجهنم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The associated report is traced through ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar to the Prophet; the author gives no grading or further wording here.
rows.anchor: حديثا من طريق عبد الله بن عمر عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet’s report says God told Adam to bring forth the fire’s contingent, and Adam produced 999 of every 1,000; “many” points toward this, though does not explicitly prove disbelievers outnumber believers.
rows.anchor: قال الله لآدم أخرج بعث النار فأخرج من كل ألف تسعة وتسعين وتسعمائة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers are described as failing to understand with their hearts, see with their eyes, and hear with their ears; fiqh means understanding.
rows.anchor: وصفت هذه الصنيفة الكافرة المعرضة عن النظر في آيات الله بأن قلوبهم لا تفقه، والفقه الفهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse does not deny these faculties altogether, but their functioning in a particular domain, as when someone is called deaf to obscenity.
rows.anchor: وليس الغرض من ذلك نفي هذه الإدراكات عن حواسهم جملة وإنما الغرض نفيها في جهة ما

rows.speaker: مسكين الدارمي
rows.claim: Maskin al-Darimi’s poem illustrates metaphorical blindness and deafness: the speaker deliberately ignores his neighbor and what goes on between them.
rows.anchor: أعمى إذا ما جارتي خرجت ... حتى يواري جارتي الستر

rows.speaker: الآخر
rows.claim: An anonymous poet uses deafness for deliberately ignoring offensive speech, supporting the verse’s figurative description of failed perception.
rows.anchor: وعوراء الكلام صممت عنها ... ولو أني أشاء بها سميع

rows.speaker: الآخر
rows.claim: Another anonymous poet’s instruction is to enter a king’s house blind and leave it mute, another figurative use of sensory incapacity.
rows.anchor: وادخل إذا ما دخلت أعمى ... واخرج إذا ما خرجت أخرس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because these people did not benefit from reflection or from the signs and admonitions they heard, they deserved the description of not understanding, seeing, or hearing.
rows.anchor: لما لم ينفعهم النظر بالقلب ولا بالعين ولا ما سمعوه من الآيات والمواعظ

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid explains the hearts as failing to grasp anything about the Hereafter, the eyes as failing to see guidance, and the ears as failing to hear truth.
rows.anchor: وفسر مجاهد هذا بأن قال: لهم قلوب لا يفقهون بها شيئا من أمر الآخرة وأعين لا يبصرون بها الهدى وآذان لا يسمعون بها الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Those” points back to the disbelievers already mentioned; cattle cannot understand things or reason by analogy, and what they see does not yield proper knowledge, as with these people.
rows.anchor: وأولئك إشارة إلى من تقدم ذكره من الكفرة وشبههم بالأنعام في أن الأنعام لا تفقه قلوبهم الأشياء ولا تعقل المقاييس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humans are more astray than cattle because cattle fulfill their created nature, while humans have understanding and means of reasoning but negligence and refusal make them resemble cattle.
rows.anchor: وهؤلاء معدون للفهم وقد خلقت لهم قوى يصرفونها وأعطوا طرقا في النظر فهم بغفلتهم وإعراضهم يلحقون أنفسهم بالأنعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing description “heedless” identifies the route by which they became more astray: heedlessness and neglect.
rows.anchor: ثم بين بقوله: أولئك هم الغافلون الطريق الذي به صاروا أضل من الأنعام وهو الغفلة والتقصير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reported occasion says Abu Jahl heard the Prophet’s companions invoke Allah and al-Rahman in recitation, objected that Muhammad claimed one god while worshipping many, and the verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: أن أبا جهل سمع بعض أصحاب النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم يقرأ فيذكر الله في قراءته ومرة يقرأ فيذكر الرحمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exegetes agree that al-asmāʾ here means names or designations, with no viable alternative.
rows.anchor: والأسماء هنا بمعنى التسميات إجماعا من المتأولين لا يمكن غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥusnā is a verbal noun used adjectivally; alternatively it is the feminine of aḥsan, with one adjective used for a nonrational plural, as in the cited examples.
rows.anchor: والحسنى: مصدر وصف به، ويجوز أن تقدر الحسنى فعلى مؤنثه أحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The names’ goodness comes from the law authorizing and specifying their use, and also from the noble, beautiful meanings they contain.
rows.anchor: وحسن الأسماء إنما يتوجه بتحسين الشرع لإطلاقها، والنص عليها، وانضاف إلى ذلك أيضا أنها إنما تضمنت معاني حسانا شريفة

rows.speaker: ابن الباقلاني
rows.claim: Ibn al-Baqillani permits applying to God an untransmitted name that entails pure praise and has no ambiguity or association.
rows.anchor: فنص ابن الباقلاني على جواز ذلك

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن الأشعري
rows.claim: Abu al-Hasan al-Ashʿari forbids applying such an untransmitted name to God.
rows.anchor: ونص أبو الحسن الأشعري على منع ذلك

rows.speaker: الفقهاء والجمهور
rows.claim: The jurists and majority also forbid untransmitted names; Ibn ʿAtiyya prefers restricting divine names to those established by revelation, since judging pure praise without ambiguity requires rare expertise and could lead people to invent forbidden names.
rows.anchor: والفقهاء والجمهور على المنع، وهو الصواب أن لا يسمى الله تعالى إلا باسم قد أطلقته الشريعة ووقفت عليه أيضا

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One group says no agent name may be derived from Qurʾanic acts such as God mocking or plotting.
rows.anchor: فقالت فرقة: لا يطلق ذلك بوجه

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another group permits derived names only when qualified by their cause, such as “mocking the disbelievers” or “plotting against those who plot against religion.”
rows.anchor: وجوزت فرقة أن يقال ذلك مقيدا بسببه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unqualified use of such derived names is unanimously forbidden; Ibn ʿAtiyya prefers the first view because the Qurʾanic verb form suffices and no need compels the qualified alternative.
rows.anchor: وأما إطلاق ذلك دون تقييد فممنوع إجماعا، والقول الأول أقوى ولا ضرورة تدفع إلى القول الثاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine names include those in the Qurʾan and those in mutawatir hadith; these are the sources one should rely on.
rows.anchor: ومنها ما ورد في الحديث وتواتر، وهذا هو الذي ينبغي أن يعتمد عليه

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Tirmidhi report from Abu Hurayra lists ninety-nine names, some of which are anomalous; it is not mutawatir. The mutawatir wording is that whoever enumerates God’s ninety-nine names enters Paradise.
rows.anchor: وقد ورد في الترمذي حديث عن أبي هريرة ونص فيه تسعة وتسعين اسما، وفي بعضها شذوذ وذلك الحديث ليس بالمتواتر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Enumerating the names means counting and memorizing them, believing in them, revering them, aspiring through them, and reflecting on their meanings.
rows.anchor: ومعنى أحصاها عدها وحفظها وتضمن ذلك الإيمان بها والتعظيم لها والرغبة فيها والعبرة في معانيها

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A prophetic supplication includes the names “O Ḥannān, O Mannān,” which do not occur in al-Tirmidhi’s list.
rows.anchor: «يا حنان يا منان» ولم يقع هذان الاسمان في تسمية الترمذي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Call upon Him by them” grants permission to invoke God using these names.
rows.anchor: فادعوه بها إباحة بإطلاقها

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd takes “leave those” to mean leave them without arguing or confronting them; on this interpretation the verse was abrogated by fighting.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد: معناه اتركوهم ولا تحاجوهم ولا تعرضوا لهم، فالآية على هذا منسوخة بالقتال

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the wording as a threat, comparable to the cited commands to leave the guilty to eat and enjoy themselves.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه الوعيد كقوله تعالى: ذرني ومن خلقت وحيدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alhada and lahada both mean to deviate, incline, or turn aside; alhada is more common, and the author cites an anonymous line using al-mulḥid.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول الشاعر: [الرجز] ليس الإمام بالشحيح الملحد قال أبو علي

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu ʿAli says the form under discussion is scarcely heard in usage.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: ولا يكاد يسمع لأحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author connects the root to the Qurʾanic phrase “with deviation” and to the grave’s sideward niche (laḥd).
rows.anchor: وفي القرآن ومن يرد فيه بإلحاد [الحج: 25] ومنه لحد القبر المائل إلى أحد شقيه

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وابن كثير ونافع وعاصم وابن عامر
rows.claim: These readers pronounce yalḥidūna with yāʾ ḍamma and ḥāʾ kasra, likewise at the occurrences in al-Naḥl and al-Sajda.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو وابن كثير ونافع وعاصم وابن عامر «يلحدون» بضم الياء وكسر الحاء، وكذلك في النحل والسجدة

rows.speaker: حمزة وابن وثاب وطلحة وعيسى والأعمش
rows.claim: Hamza reads all three occurrences with yāʾ and ḥāʾ fatḥa; Ibn Waththab, Talha, ʿIsa, and al-Aʿmash do likewise.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة الأحرف الثلاثة «يلحدون» بفتح الياء والحاء، وكذلك ابن وثاب وطلحة وعيسى والأعمش

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas explains deviation in God’s names as naming al-Lat as a counterpart to Allah.
rows.anchor: أن يسموا اللات نظيرا إلى اسم الله تعالى قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid explains the practice as naming al-ʿUzza as a counterpart to al-ʿAziz.
rows.anchor: والعزى نظيرا إلى العزيز، قاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another form of deviation is calling God “Lord” while calling idols “lords.”
rows.anchor: ويسمون الله ربا ويسمون أوثانهم أربابا ونحو هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise that they will be recompensed is an unqualified threat of punishment in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: سيجزون ما كانوا يعملون وعيد محض بعذاب الآخرة

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi distinguishes alhada as meaning to deviate from lahada as meaning to lean or seek refuge.
rows.anchor: وذهب الكسائي إلى الفرق بين ألحد ولحد وزعم أن ألحد بمعنى مال وانحرف ولحد بمعنى ركن وانضوى

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi reads all Qurʾanic occurrences with yāʾ ḍamma and ḥāʾ kasra except al-Naḥl, which he reads with both vowels open as “leaning”; Abu ʿAli transmits the same account.
rows.anchor: قال الطبري: وكان الكسائي يقرأ جميع ما في القرآن بضم الياء وكسر الحاء إلا التي في النحل فإنه كان يقرؤها بفتح الياء والحاء

rows.speaker: مجاهد وغيره
rows.claim: Mujahid and others take the scene as a striking disclosure of what befell the disbelievers at Badr, and a warning to those who remained.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية تتضمن التعجيب مما حل بالكفار يوم بدر، قاله مجاهد وغيره، وفي ذلك وعيد لمن بقي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional law has no stated apodosis, creating a powerful ambiguity.
rows.anchor: وحذف جواب، لو إبهام بليغ

rows.speaker: جمهور السبعة والناس
rows.claim: The majority of the Seven and other readers read yatwaffā with yāʾ; masculine marking is acceptable before the grammatically feminine word because the referent is not feminine in reality.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جمهور السبعة والناس «يتوفى» بالياء فعل فيه علامة التذكير إلى مؤنث في اللفظ، وساغ ذلك أن التأنيث غير حقيقي

rows.speaker: بعض من قرأ هذه القراءة
rows.claim: Some readers construe God as the subject of “takes”; “the angels” is then a nominative topic, with “they strike” as its predicate and the clause circumstantial.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض من قرأ هذه القراءة إن المعنى إذ يتوفى الله الذين كفروا والملائكة رفع بالابتداء، ويضربون خبره والجملة في موضع الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya finds that construction weak because the circumstantial clause lacks the wāw that is generally required in such a structure.
rows.anchor: ويضعف هذا التأويل سقوط واو الحال فإنها في الأغلب تلزم مثل هذا

rows.speaker: ابن عامر والأعرج
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAmir and al-Aʿraj read tatawaffā with tāʾ, making the angels the subject; “they strike” is circumstantial.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر من السبعة والأعرج «تتوفى» بالتاء على الإسناد إلى لفظ «الملائكة»

rows.speaker: جمهور المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes understand “their backsides” euphemistically as their anuses, while God uses a decorous expression.
rows.anchor: قال جمهور المفسرين يريد أستاههم، ولكن الله كريم كنى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas instead takes the phrase as their backs and what was behind them; the angels catch and strike them as they flee, while their faces are struck when they face forward.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أراد ظهورهم وما أدبر منهم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reports that a man noticed a whip-like mark on Abu Jahl’s back, and the Prophet said it was a blow from the angels.
rows.anchor: وروى الحسن أن رجلا قال: يا رسول الله رأيت في ظهر أبي جهل مثل الشراك، فقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «ذلك ضرب الملائكة»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels are spoken of in the plural although the Angel of Death is one, because he has angelic assistants.
rows.anchor: وعبر بجمع الملائكة، وملك الموت واحد إذ له على ذلك أعوان من الملائكة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One reading of “taste the punishment of burning” is that the angels said these words at the time, with “they say” omitted for brevity.
rows.anchor: قيل كانوا يقولون للكفار حينئذ هذا اللفظ فحذف يقولون اختصار

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another reading places the words at the Resurrection, when the disbelievers will be told this.
rows.anchor: وقيل معناه وحالهم يوم القيامة أن يقال لهم هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥarīq is an adjective on the faʿīl pattern from ḥaraq, burning.
rows.anchor: والحريق فعيل من الحرق

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: “That is because of what your hands have sent” may be the angels’ words as they take the disbelievers in the described manner.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن يكون من قول الملائكة في وقت توفيتهم لهم على الصورة المذكورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, it may be a new rebuke from God directed to disbelievers, both living and dead.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون كلاما مستأنفا تقريعا من الله عز وجل للكافرين حيهم وميتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase can be nominative by supplying “the judgment is that,” or genitive by coordination with the mā in “because of what your hands sent.”
rows.anchor: وأن يصح أن تكون في موضع رفع على تقدير والحكم أن، ويصح أن تكون في موضع خفض عطفا على ما في قوله بما قدمت

rows.speaker: مكي والزهراوي
rows.claim: Makki and al-Zahrawi also allow an accusative construction by dropping the preposition bāʾ, understood as “and because.”
rows.anchor: وقال مكي والزهراوي: ويصح أن تكون في موضع نصب بإسقاط الباء تقديره «وبأن»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya rejects the proposed accusative analysis of “that” as unclear unless a verb is supplied implicitly.
rows.anchor: وهذا غير متجه ولا بين إلا أن تنصب بإضمار فعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Daʾb means customary practice in Arabic; the author cites Imruʾ al-Qays’s line, with a transmitted variant reading dīnik in place of daʾbik.
rows.anchor: كدأبك من أم الحويرث قبلها ... وجارتها أم الرباب بمأسل

rows.speaker: خراش بن زهير العامري
rows.claim: Kharash ibn Zuhayr al-ʿAmiri’s verse also uses daʾb for a continuing customary course.
rows.anchor: فما زال ذاك الدأب حتى تخاذلت ... هوازن وارفضت سليم وعامر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word derives from persisting in work; the Prophet told a camel’s owner that the camel complained he starved and overworked it, illustrating sustained toil.
rows.anchor: وهو مأخوذ من دأب على العمل إذا لزمه، ومنه قول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، لصاحب الجمل

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet told the camel’s owner that the animal complained of being starved and worked hard.
rows.anchor: إنه شكا إلي أنك تجيعه وتدئبه

rows.speaker: جابر بن زيد وعامر الشعبي ومجاهد وعطاء
rows.claim: Jabir ibn Zayd, ʿAmir al-Shaʿbi, Mujahid, and ʿAtaʾ gloss the verse as the ways of Pharaoh’s people.
rows.anchor: وقال جابر بن زيد وعامر الشعبي ومجاهد وعطاء: المعنى كسنن آل فرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It may mean the customary course of Pharaoh’s people and the other nations collectively, since each nation was destroyed once rather than Pharaoh’s people being destroyed repeatedly.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يراد كعادة آل فرعون وغيرهم، فتكون عادة الأمم بجملتها لا على انفراد أمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It may instead mean God’s customary treatment of them, with “custom” annexed to them as either the agent or object of the verbal noun.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون المراد كعادة الله فيهم، فأضاف العادة إليهم إذ لهم نسبة إليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kāf may attach to “taste,” though this is syntactically remote; on that analysis it is an accusative modifier of an omitted verbal noun.
rows.anchor: والكاف من قوله كدأب يجوز أن يتعلق بقوله وذوقوا وفيه بعد، والكاف على هذا في موضع نصب نعت لمصدر محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kāf may instead attach to “your hands sent,” and then likewise serve as an accusative modifier of an omitted verbal noun.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن تتعلق بقوله قدمت أيديكم وموضعها أيضا على هذا نصب كما تقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the sentence may be an imperative meaning “like the practice of Pharaoh’s people,” with the kāf serving as the predicate.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون معنى الكلام الأمر مثل دأب آل فرعون فتكون الكاف في موضع خبر الابتداء

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh construes “that” as a nominative predicate, supplying “the matter is that”; another possible estimate is “that became obligatory.”
rows.anchor: ذلك في موضع رفع على خبر الابتداء تقديره عند سيبويه الأمر ذلك، ويحتمل أن يكون التقدير وجب ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ marks cause.
rows.anchor: والباء باء السبب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lam causes jussive mood and deletes the nūn in yakun; the reduced form lam yak reflects treating lam as entering directly on yakun, with deletion eased by the word’s resemblance to weak-letter forms, as in lam abal becoming lam ab.
rows.anchor: وقوله لم يك مغيرا جزم ب لم وجزمه بحذف النون، والأصل يكون فإذا دخلت لم جاء لم يكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God does not begin changing or spoiling a favor; through mercy He waits until people change their good condition by acquiring sins or disbelief, after which He turns favor into retribution.
rows.anchor: لا يبدأ بتغيرها وتكديرها حتى يجيء ذلك منهم بأن يغيروا حالهم التي تراد وتحسن منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad was a favor to Quraysh; when they disbelieved, God transferred that favor to the Ansar and brought punishment upon Quraysh.
rows.anchor: ومثال هذا نعمة الله على قريش بمحمد صلى الله عليه وسلم فكفروا ما كان يجب أن يكونوا عليه، فغير الله تلك النعمة بأن نقلها إلى غيرهم من الأنصار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “And God is hearing, knowing” means He knows everything people do in changing their inner state, whether secret or public.
rows.anchor: وسميع عليم أي لكل وبكل ما يقع من الناس في تغيير ما بأنفسهم لا يخفى عليه من ذلك سر ولا جهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the repeated comparison, the kāf attaches to “until they change”; the repetition adds a second point: the earlier comparison concerns destruction after disbelief, this one the prior change of people before a favor changes.
rows.anchor: وهذا التكرير هو لمعنى ليس للأول، إذ الأول دأب في أن هلكوا لما كفروا، وهذا الثاني دأب في أن لم تغير نعمتهم حتى غيروا ما بأنفسهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Those before them” refers to the people of Hud, Salih, Noah, Shuʿayb, and others.
rows.anchor: والإشارة بقوله الذين من قبلهم إلى قوم هود وصالح ونوح وشعيب وغيرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The intended comparison makes even vile animals such as pigs and vicious dogs better than disbelievers whom God has decreed will never believe; a disbeliever who later believes is not the worst of creatures.
rows.anchor: المعنى المقصود تفضيل الدواب الذميمة كالخنزير والكلب العقور على الكافرين الذين حتم عليهم بأنهم لا يؤمنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative clause may identify the worst beasts as disbelievers who remain in disbelief and repeatedly break covenants, giving three traits; alternatively it resumes the earlier “those,” meaning a group made treaty and then broke it.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن يريد أن الموصوف ب شر الدواب هم الذين لا يؤمنون المعاهدون من الكفار فكانوا شر الدواب على هذا بثلاثة أوصاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The treaty here means making peace and refraining from war.
rows.anchor: والمعاهدة في هذه الآية المسالمة وترك الحرب

rows.speaker: المتأولون
rows.claim: Exegetes agree that the verse was revealed about Banu Qurayza, while its rule applies through the end of time to anyone with the same traits.
rows.anchor: وأجمع المتأولون أن الآية نزلت في بني قريظة، وهي بعد تعم كل من اتصف بهذه الصفة إلى يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reducing “beasts” to human beings alone fails to convey the full condemnation: the word covers people and other animals, and its broad use completes the reproach.
rows.anchor: ومن قال إن المراد ب الدواب الناس فقول لا يستوفي المذمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Every time” entails that their treachery had occurred repeatedly before.
rows.anchor: وقوله في كل مرة يقتضي أن الغدر قد كان وقع منهم وتكرر ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Banu Qurayza had agreed not to fight the Prophet or aid another enemy; when the confederates gathered at Medina they expected his defeat, and Huyayy ibn Akhtab deceived their leader Kaʿb ibn Asad into breaking the pact and supplying Quraysh with arms and armor.
rows.anchor: غلب على ظن بني قريظة أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، مغلوب ومستأصل، وخدع حيي بن أخطب النضري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the crisis passed, God ordered the Prophet to fight them; they surrendered and were executed under Saʿd ibn Muʿadh’s judgment.
rows.anchor: فلما انجلت تلك الحال عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، أمره الله بالخروج إليهم وحربهم فاستنزلوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is Medinan except for the two closing verses beginning “A messenger has come to you” and continuing to its end.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة مدنية إلا آيتين: لقد جاءكم رسول [التوبة: 128] إلى آخرها

rows.speaker: حذيفة وغيره
rows.claim: The surah is called al-Tawba; the text associates this title with Hudhayfa and others.
rows.anchor: فاله حذيفة وغيره، وتسمى الفاضحة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas reports that it is also called al-Faḍiḥa, “the exposer.”
rows.anchor: وتسمى الفاضحة قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is also called al-Ḥāfira because it dug into and exposed the hypocrites’ hearts.
rows.anchor: وتسمى الحافرة لأنها حفرت عن قلوب المنافقين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says the repeated revelations identifying people as “among them” continued until he thought no one would remain unexposed.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس مازال ينزل ومنهم ومنهم حتى ظن أنه لا يبقى أحد

rows.speaker: حذيفة
rows.claim: Hudhayfa calls it the surah of punishment.
rows.anchor: وقال حذيفة: هي سورة العذاب

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar says they called it al-Mufashfisha.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عمر كنا ندعوها المفشفشة

rows.speaker: الحارث بن يزيد
rows.claim: Al-Harith ibn Yazid says it was called al-Mubaththira; other names given are al-Muthira and al-Buhuth.
rows.anchor: قال الحارث بن يزيد: كانت تدعى المبعثرة ويقال لها المثيرة، ويقال لها البحوث

rows.speaker: أبو مالك الغفاري
rows.claim: Abu Malik al-Ghifari says the first verse revealed from al-Tawba was “March forth, lightly and heavily.”
rows.anchor: وقال أبو مالك الغفاري: أول آية نزلت من براءة انفروا خفافا وثقالا [التوبة: 41]

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr says al-Tawba was as long as al-Baqara.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير: كانت براءة مثل سورة البقرة في الطول

rows.speaker: عثمان بن عفان
rows.claim: ʿUthman explains that the basmala was omitted because al-Tawba’s themes resembled al-Anfal; the two were treated as a pair in the Prophet’s time, placed together among the seven long surahs, and left without the basmala.
rows.anchor: فقال عثمان بن عفان أشبهت معانيها معاني الأنفال وكانت تدعى القرينتين في زمن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: ʿAli says the basmala signals safety and good news, whereas al-Tawba came with the sword and repudiation of treaties, so it did not open with that assurance; Ibn ʿAtiyya says this is ʿAli’s view, though attributed to al-Mubarrad, and compares the tone to an angry speaker beginning “amma baʿd.”
rows.anchor: وقال علي بن أبي طالب لابن عباس رضي الله عنهما: بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم أمان وبشارة، وبراءة نزلت بالسيف ونبذ العهود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya attributes the explanation to ʿAli rather than al-Mubarrad and compares it to an angry speaker who begins “as for what follows” without praise or honorific opening.
rows.anchor: ويعزى هذا القول للمبرد وهو لعلي بن أبي طالب رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the codex scribes differed over whether al-Anfal and al-Tawba were one surah or two, they left a separation but omitted the basmala to accommodate both positions.
rows.anchor: فتركوا فصلا بينهما مراعاة لقول من قال هما سورتان ولم يكتبوا بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم مراعاة لقول من قال منهم هما واحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya considers that account weak because it would mean the Qurʾan’s arrangement was left disputed in this way.
rows.anchor: وهذا القول يضعفه النظر أن يختلف في كتاب الله هكذا

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb says the Prophet ordered them to put the basmala at the start of each surah but gave no instruction for this one, so they did not place it.
rows.anchor: وروي عن أبي بن كعب أنه قال: كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يأمرنا بوضع بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم في أول كل سورة

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik says it reached him that the surah was once as long as al-Baqara, then much of it was abrogated and lifted, including the basmala; they therefore avoided putting the basmala in a place where it did not belong.
rows.anchor: وروي عن مالك أنه قال: بلغنا أنها كانت نحو سورة البقرة ثم نسخ ورفع كثير منها وفيه البسملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tawba was among the last revelations; an anecdote has a Bedouin infer this from its references to omissions and repudiated treaties.
rows.anchor: وسورة براءة من آخر ما نزل على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، وحكى عمران بن جدير أن أعرابيا سمع سورة براءة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun “some of them” refers to hypocrites; when a surah exposing their secrets was revealed, they signaled one another to ask whether anyone was watching or could report them.
rows.anchor: الضمير في قوله بعضهم عائد على المنافقين، والمعنى وإذا ما أنزلت سورة فيها فضيحة أسرارهم نظر بعضهم إلى بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Then they turned away” means they turned from guidance: exposure provoked a pause suited to reflection, but their persistence in disbelief made them turn from the moment that could have led to guidance; the wording counts their sin.
rows.anchor: فهم إذ يصممون على الكفر ويرتبكون فيه كأنهم انصرفوا عن تلك الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “God turned their hearts” may be a curse against them or a statement that they deserved this because they did not understand God or His Messenger.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن يكون دعاء عليهم، ويحتمل أن يكون خبرا أي استوجبوا ذلك بأنهم قوم لا يفقهون

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Tabari reports Ibn ʿAbbas warning against saying “we turned away from prayer,” since people who turned away had their hearts turned by God; instead say “we completed the prayer.”
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أنه قال: لا تقولوا انصرفنا من الصلاة فإن قوما انصرفوا فصرف الله قلوبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here naẓar is a gesture or signal; al-Tabari also reports an unnamed view that it means “said.”
rows.anchor: فهذا النظر الذي في هذه الآية هو إيماء، وحكى الطبري عن بعضهم أنه قال: نظر في هذه الآية في موضع قال

rows.speaker: جمهور
rows.claim: The majority take the address as directed to the Arabs, enumerating God’s favor in sending them a messenger who spoke their language and conveyed eloquent meanings they understood, giving them enduring honor.
rows.anchor: مخاطبة للعرب في قول الجمهور وهذا على جهة تعديد النعمة عليهم في ذلك، إذ جاء بلسانهم وبما يفهمونه من الأغراض والفصاحة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj takes the address as directed to all humanity, with the sense that a human messenger came to them; Ibn ʿAtiyya prefers the majority’s reading.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: هي مخاطبة لجميع العالم، والمعنى لقد جاءكم رسول من البشر والأول أصوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “From among yourselves” praises the Prophet’s lineage as being from the heart of Arab nobility, supported by the report that God chose Kinana from Ishmael’s descendants, Quraysh from Kinana, Banu Hashim from Quraysh, and the Prophet from Banu Hashim.
rows.anchor: إن الله اصطفى كنانة من ولد إسماعيل، واصطفى قريشا من كنانة، واصطفى بني هاشم من قريش، واصطفاني من بني هاشم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet says he is from legitimate marriage rather than fornication, meaning his ancestry back to Adam contained no illicit parentage.
rows.anchor: ومنه قوله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «إني من نكاح ولست من سفاح» معناه أن نسبه صلى الله عليه وسلم إلى آدم عليه السلام لم يكن النسل فيه إلا من نكاح

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن قسيط المكي
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allah ibn Qusayt al-Makki reads “min anfusikum” with fāʾ fatḥa, making it mean “from among your most precious”; the reading is also transmitted from the Prophet and Fatima, with Ibn ʿAbbas reporting it from the Prophet according to Abu ʿAmr.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله بن قسيط المكي «من أنفسكم» بفتح الفاء من النفاسة، ورويت عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وعن فاطمة رضي الله عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “what has burdened you is grievous to him,” mā can be a verbal noun as the initial subject with ʿazīz as fronted predicate; alternatively it can be the subject of ʿazīz, which is an adjective for the Messenger. Ibn ʿAtiyya prefers the latter syntax.
rows.anchor: ما عنتم فاعلا ب عزيز وعزيز صفة للرسول، وهذا أصوب من الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAnat means hardship and broadly includes what burdens people in disbelief and misguidance, as well as being killed, captured, or tested for the truth and their belief.
rows.anchor: والعنت المشقة وهي هنا لفظة عامة أي ما شق عليكم من كفر وضلال بحسب الحق ومن قتل أو أسار وامتحان بسبب الحق

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada takes the phrase specifically to mean hardship borne by the believers among the audience.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: المعنى عنت مؤمنيكم
